message.content:
Below is an overview of key protections and responsibilities you have as a residential tenant in Texas (as of May 2026). **This is general information only—if you’re facing a particular dispute or need tailored guidance, consult a licensed attorney or your local housing agency.** | Topic | What You Can Expect / Your Rights | |-------|-----------------------------------| | **Security Deposit Limits** | • Landlords may charge up to *one month’s rent* if the lease term ≤ 12 months;
• Up to *two months’ rent* if > 12 months.
*No interest is required.* | | **Deposit Return & Deductions** | • Must be returned within **30 days** after tenancy ends unless written agreement says otherwise.
• Landlord may keep money only for:
  - Unpaid rent
  - Damage beyond normal wear‑and‑tear
  - Cleaning costs if agreed upon in writing
• Tenant receives itemized statement of deductions. | | **Notice Requirements** | • **Month‑to‑month:** 30‑day written notice from either party.
• **Fixed‑term leases:** Notice period specified in lease; usually at least 30 days before termination.
• For **eviction**, landlord must serve proper notices per §92.005–92.015 (e.g., pay‑or‑quit, cure‑or‑quit). | | **Habitability & Repairs** | • Landlord must maintain premises in “habitably” condition under Texas Property Code §§91.001–91.009.
• Tenants must promptly report needed repairs; landlords generally responsible for major structural issues, plumbing, heating/cooling, electrical safety, pest control, etc.
• If landlord fails to repair, tenants may:
 1) Pay for repair themselves and deduct cost from rent (after giving notice),
 2) Withhold rent until repaired (but risk eviction),
 3) Terminate lease if conditions become uninhabitable. | | **Rent Increases** | • No statutory cap on increases; however, they must be disclosed in advance via written notice (usually 30 days prior). | | **Privacy & Entry** | • Landlord must give reasonable notice (typically 24 hours) before entering except emergencies.
• Reasonable entry times are typically during daylight hours. | | **Discrimination Protections** | • Under federal Fair Housing Act and Texas Civil Rights Act, discrimination based on race, color, religion, sex, national origin, disability, familial status, age, marital status, source of income, or other protected classes is prohibited. | | **Lease Terms & Modifications** | • Written agreements govern most matters; oral modifications are enforceable only if both parties agree. | | **Evictions** | • Common grounds: Nonpayment of rent, violation of lease terms, illegal activity, property damage, or owner’s intent to occupy.
• Process: Serve notice → File unlawful detainer action → Court judgment → Sheriff enforcement. | | **Tenant Remedies** | • If evicted without due process, you may sue for damages or seek injunctions.
• If landlord breaches lease (fails to repair, violates privacy, wrongfully raises rent), you may file complaint with the Texas Attorney General’s Office or local consumer protection office. | ### Quick Reference Resources | Resource | Where to Find It | |----------|------------------| | **Texas Property Code** | State Legislature website – [https://statutes.capitol.texas.gov/](https://statutes.capitol.texas.gov/) | | **Fair Housing Laws** | U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development – HUD.gov | | **Local Rent Control Ordinances** | City/Town official websites (not all cities in TX have them) | | **Consumer Protection Complaint Forms** | Texas Attorney General Consumer Protection Division – [https://www.txcpa.state.tx.us/consumer-protection](https://www.txcpa.state.tx.us/consumer-protection) | | **Legal Aid Clinics** | Local bar association directories or community law centers | --- #### Bottom Line As a Texas tenant: 1. **Know your lease** – read it carefully; understand what the landlord can legally do and when you can terminate. 2. **Document everything** – photos, emails, text messages, receipts for repairs. 3. **Communicate in writing** whenever possible (especially regarding maintenance requests or disputes). 4. **Act quickly** if something becomes unsafe or if you believe your rights were violated. If you encounter a problem (e.g., unjustified rent increase, failure to fix essential services, wrongful eviction notice), start by contacting the landlord in writing, then consider filing a formal complaint with the appropriate state or local authority, or seeking free/legal aid counsel.
